title: Ahead of the Patient
concept: Alaska hospitals in the volunteer Alaska Stroke Coalition use RapidAI to read stroke scans. It flags a suspected large vessel occlusion, and in one case it alerted the doctor seconds after the scan, with the results reaching the local team and the clot specialists at once, in a state with five doctors who can pull out those clots. Before, just sending the images to Anchorage could take 45 minutes. In another case a man in his sixties came into an interior hospital after a fall; his team called Providence in Anchorage under 30 minutes after he arrived, two minutes before the official scan report, and the clot was out 4 hours 23 minutes after he arrived. Early, unpublished data shows about a 30 percent faster start on clot removal once patients reach Anchorage. The test: Providence's Kelly Isaacs says she can't really show statistically significant proof, Alaska has no consistent stroke outcome reporting, the software throws false positives; the clinicians' answer is that a doctor reviews every output and decides the transfer, and the six hospitals that got it free say they'll keep and pay. Federal rural health money, over $3.1 million, is set to build an AI imaging network across a planned 21 hospitals. Drawn as Ping, a round orchid alert pulse with a face born in a CT ring, that splits so the news reaches two places at once; in the second case a slow faceless report printer loses to a phone call; the film ends on a scoreboard whose outcomes row is a dashed blank.

divergence_note: The last three films were outdoors: a hard low noon sun on bone snow at a rail fork with a faceless cast-iron switch stand and signal amber (11-25), flat July overcast on olive tundra seen from above with a faced Pi board and red pins (11-24), and apricot-plum dusk on river ice with scarlet and sample tubes (11-23). This film is a screen-lit hospital interior before dawn, celadon tile and graphite-teal under a bone lightbox key; its hero is a round faced orchid pulse that splits (no card or document silhouette); its accent is orchid at about 318 degrees, about 50 degrees from 11-24's vermilion and 11-23's scarlet and far from 11-25's amber. Honest overlaps: a stylised Alaska map board seen from above in two shots (11-23 and 11-24 used top-down maps), a faceless Suit (house rig), and a brass stopwatch from the 11-19 shelf.

treatment.title: Ahead of the Patient
treatment.summary: Winner A (the Comedian, Ping) with grafts from C (the Explainer: the split-screen of a gurney token still on the dashed line while Anchorage's room is already lit, the brass brain-cell counter), B (the Dramatist: the button pulls back through the CT ring so the last frame rhymes with the first) and D (the Enthusiast: the dashed OUTCOMES row, six separate hospital vignettes lighting for keep and pay). Case one is an unplaced Alaska hospital (a CT room, a reading room, a lightbox, a wall phone). Case two is a DIFFERENT hospital in the interior (its own exterior doors in the blue before sunrise, its own intake board, desk phone and slow faceless report printer). Then a records shelf, a doctor's desk, six separate hospital vignettes, a long dusk horizon of Alaska, and the Anchorage stroke room. Ping, a round faced orchid alert pulse born in the CT ring, is the protagonist: it reads, flags, splits into two identical copies, races ahead of the patient, gets checked by a doctor's pen, and ends trying to hang its stopwatch on a RESULTS nail where an empty dashed scoreboard waits. Revised after Gate 0B/0C/0D round 1: Ping is a round pulse, not a card; orchid replaces coral; the clot is drawn as a vessel cutoff with a tiny ruby marker; the second case has its own world and its own printer and phone with no orchid on them; the specialists never sit on the map; the split race is a general diagram after the case; the network is a horizon, not a third map; the six hospitals are six separate vignettes.
treatment.judge_reasoning: Judge reasoning: all four pitches converged on the same physics (one alert that splits so the local team and the specialists learn at once, a stopwatch, a report that arrives second, a blank outcomes scoreboard), so the judgment is about who makes it a show. The Comedian's Ping is the only pitch whose AI presence is a character with a face that FEELS each beat (born, proud, splitting, sheepish at a false positive, deflated at the empty nail), and its slow faceless report printer is a running background gag that pays off on c15 at the exact beat. Grafts: from the Explainer, the split-screen signature shot (a gurney token still crawling the dashed line on the left, Anchorage's room already lighting on the right: the information racing ahead of the patient) and the brass brain-cell counter; from the Dramatist, the button pulling back through the scanner ring so the last frame rhymes with the first; from the Enthusiast, the dashed OUTCOMES row and six clinic windows lighting for "keep and pay". Rejected: five specialist pins or chairs placed on the map (no claim locates them; they sit together on one WHOLE STATE card off the map), any vehicle for the patient (never flown), a 45-minutes-to-seconds before-and-after splice (c7 and c3 stay separate, "in one case" stays on c3). The showrunner judged the four pitches directly instead of spawning a separate scorer.

angle.thesis: Alaska's stroke software moves the information, not the patient: the local team and the state's specialists learn at the same moment, so Anchorage is ready before the patient arrives, and that is a real Alaska win in speed that becomes a proven one only if the planned 21-hospital network comes with the stroke outcome reporting Alaska doesn't have today.
angle.falsifiability: False if the timing gains don't hold: transfer calls still wait on the official report (c15 shows one that didn't), image delivery to specialists still takes tens of minutes (c7 is the before), or the early, unpublished faster start in Anchorage (c17) disappears once published. Also false, in its second half, if Alaska can already judge the network without new reporting (contradicting c20, c21).
supporting_facts: The mechanism is information: just sending images to Anchorage could take 45 minutes (c7); in one case the app alerted the doctor seconds after the scan (c3) and the results reached the local team and the faraway specialists at once (c4).

One real chain: a man in his mid-60s after a morning fall at an interior hospital (c13), the transfer call under 30 minutes after arrival (c14), two minutes before the official report (c15), the clot out 4 hours 23 minutes after he arrived (c16).

The payoff lands in Anchorage: early, unpublished data shows about a 30 percent faster start on clot removal once patients get there (c17), with five clot specialists in the entire state (c6) and about two million brain cells lost a minute without blood flow (c5).
angle.counterpoint_to_honor: Two fair cases, each a scene. The skeptic's: no one can show it changes outcomes yet; Isaacs says she can't really give statistically significant proof (c21), the state has no consistent outcome reporting (c20), the software throws false positives (c18). The clinicians' answer, shown straight as the best reason the bet is sound: a doctor still reviews every output and that read decides the transfer (c19), they didn't put it in to send every patient to Anchorage (c22), and all six hospitals that got it free say they'll keep and pay for it (c10).
angle.valence_defense: The capability is measured in minutes and it's Alaska-built (a volunteer coalition c24, foundation money c9, now federal money c11 toward a planned 21 hospitals c12). The film lets that land as a win and names exactly one honest limit, the missing outcome scoreboard, as the condition for calling it proven. No invented downside.
angle.who_it_serves: Rural and interior Alaskans who have a stroke far from a cath lab, their local ER teams, the five specialists, and the officials deciding how federal rural health money is judged.
angle.second_movement: c17 recontextualises the case: the gain the data sees shows up in Anchorage, because the information got there first. Then the test: Isaacs's own question (c21) and c20, met by c19, c22 and c10.

hook.frame1: A cold CT room, a greyscale slice in the bore whose bright vessel already stops at a cutoff, and at 0.2 s Ping pops awake in front of it with a squash and a PING while the ring's lamps chase round
hook.headline: A BRAIN SCAN · AN ALASKA HOSPITAL
hook.loopback: Frame 1 is Ping waking in the CT bore beside a bare RESULTS nail; the last shot pulls back out through the same bore to frame Ping beside the scoreboard now hung on that nail, its third row a dashed blank.

open_loop.what: What hangs on the RESULTS nail? Planted as a bare brass nail labelled RESULTS beside a cold stopwatch in the CT room; paid when the Anchorage scoreboard hangs on the nail and Ping tugs the taped paper off its OUTCOMES row on camera to show a dashed blank under the lit TIME rows.

open_loop_2.what: Will the five get called for nothing? Planted as one of the five figures' pagers twitches on its belt while Ping counts them; paid when Ping yells at a clear slice and that pager blinks, then the doctor's read flips a slip to CLEAR · NO TRANSFER CALL and the pager goes dark: false positives, and a doctor's read decides the transfer.
